title: Romance of the Sui and Tang Dynasties
subtitle: Wagang Heroes Rise from Every Quarter · Eighteen Rebel Kings Shake Sui and Tang
description: Romance of the Sui and Tang Dynasties is a full-length historical novel by the Qing-dynasty writer Chu Renhuo, comprising one hundred chapters. It narrates the rise and fall of dynasties over more than 170 years, from Emperor Wen of Sui's campaign against Chen to Emperor Xuanzong of Tang's An Lushan Rebellion. The story centers on the legendary exploits of the Wagang heroes — Qin Qiong, Cheng Yaojin, Yuchi Gong — interspersed with major historical events such as Emperor Yang of Sui's visit to Yangzhou and Emperor Taizong of Tang's Zhenguan Golden Age. It is hailed as an encyclopedia of Sui-Tang history.

route.title: Romance of the Sui and Tang Dynasties: A Golden Age of Heroes Amid the Clash of Storms
route.intro:
Misty willows on the Sui dikes, spring breezes in the Tang gardens. Qin Qiong sells his horse, Yuchi Gong wrests the spear — on Wagang Stockade the heroes gather.
Chu Renhuo (1635–1703), style name Jiaxuan, literary name Stone Farmer, was a native of Changzhou, Jiangsu (modern Suzhou). A man of wide learning, he melded official history, unofficial histories, novels, and operas into a single magnificent historical tapestry of the Sui and Tang dynasties. Qin Qiong's righteousness, Cheng Yaojin's simple-heartedness, Luo Cheng's courage, Li Yuanba's ferocity — these vivid characters have been deeply etched into the cultural memory of the Chinese people. Let us follow the footsteps of the Wagang heroes — from the Jinci Temple in Taiyuan to the Daming Palace in Chang'an, from the Longmen Grottoes in Luoyang to the Grand Canal in Yangzhou — visiting the national heritage sites that bear witness to the glory of the Sui-Tang golden age and the legends of its heroes.

stops.title: Stop One: Taiyuan · The Land Where the Dragon Rose
stops.content: In the thirteenth year of Daye (617 AD), Li Yuan raised the standard of revolt against the Sui in Taiyuan, beginning the three-hundred-year foundation of the Tang dynasty. It was from here that his son Li Shimin set out on the path to conquer the realm — recruiting Qin Qiong, subduing Yuchi Gong, defeating Liu Wuzhou. Taiyuan was truly the land where the Tang dragon rose. Nestled at the foot of Xuanweng Mountain, the Jinci Temple was recorded as early as Li Daoyuan's Commentary on the Water Classic in the Northern Wei. Built to honor Tang Shuyu, it is where Emperor Taizong of Tang personally composed the "Inscription and Preface for Jinci Temple." This garden is not only a microcosm of the long-standing culture of the Three Jin region but also a living fossil of the founding history of the Tang dynasty. The Song-dynasty painted clay statues of palace maids in the Hall of the Holy Mother and the inexhaustible Nanlao Spring have witnessed the dramatic transitions from the Taiyuan uprising to the Zhenguan Golden Age. The Jinci Temple (originally Tang Shuyu Temple) is the earliest surviving imperial sacrificial garden, its building complex spanning the Song, Jin, Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties. The Hall of the Holy Mother was built in the Tiansheng reign of the Northern Song. Seven bays wide and six bays deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, it is surrounded by a pillared cloister — one of the earliest surviving ancient Chinese buildings with an encircling corridor. Before the hall stand eight coiling-dragon columns, each bearing a carved wooden dragon spiraling upward, claws spread wide, whiskers flying — after nearly a thousand years, the eight dragons still seem about to burst from the columns and take flight. The forty-three Song-dynasty painted clay maidens within the hall are also peerless: some hold seals, some carry fans, some bow their heads, some smile — they are not deities but living Song-dynasty court ladies frozen in clay. Standing before them, you can feel the warmth of the Northern Song craftsmen's hands. Li Shimin's "Inscription and Preface for Jinci Temple" was written in his own hand in the twentieth year of Zhenguan (646 AD). After pacifying the Turks, he returned to Taiyuan and visited Jinci Temple to pay homage to Tang Shuyu. The inscription reads: "The founding achievement of the former king could not have been established without the virtue of Tang Shuyu; the glory of succeeding generations could not have been accomplished without the enterprise of Wu Zhou." He traced the foundation of the Tang dynasty back three thousand years to Tang Shuyu, and gave thanks for the power this land of Taiyuan had given him. The Nanlao Spring at Jinci Temple gushes from the rock face, its waters abundant and never-failing for a thousand years — the cool sound of the spring and the ding-dong of wind chimes at the eaves interweave in a music that has been playing for over a millennium. From the road of Taiyuan where Prince of Qin Li Shimin once rode with spear and horse, to the Jinci Temple graced by the imperial brush of the Zhenguan Emperor — one man's growth and one dynasty's rise are both crystallized in this garden of flowing springs.

stops.title: Stop Two: Chang'an · The Heavenly Qaghan of the Great Tang
stops.content: The Tang dynasty made Chang'an its capital, beginning the most glorious chapter in Chinese history. After Li Shimin ascended the throne, he listened humbly to advice, and the Zhenguan Golden Age brought peace and prosperity — "Using bronze as a mirror, one can straighten one's clothes and cap; using history as a mirror, one can understand the cycle of rise and fall." Qin Qiong and Yuchi Gong, armed and armored, guarded the Xuanwu Gate. These two battle-hardened generals who had emerged from Wagang Stockade ultimately became the guardian spirits of Chang'an, and later were elevated by the people into door gods. The Daming Palace Ruins cover 3.2 square kilometers, with the foundations of the Hanyuan Hall and Linde Hall still visible — this was the most magnificent palace complex of the Tang dynasty and the most splendid architectural ensemble in the world at the time. And the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda rises in the southern part of the city, a witness to Xuanzang's return from his scripture quest and a symbol of how the light of civilization continued to shine after the heroes' tales of the Sui and Tang had drawn to a close. Standing on the Daming Palace ruins and gazing at the silhouette of the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, you can almost hear the resounding voices of the emperor and his ministers debating state policy in the Zhenguan court. The Daming Palace Ruins were the heart of the Tang empire, built in the eighth year of Zhenguan (634 AD), covering 3.2 square kilometers — four times the size of the Forbidden City in Beijing. The Hanyuan Hall was the main hall of the palace, its foundation rising fifteen meters above ground, 75.9 meters from east to west and 41.3 meters from north to south — standing on the foundation and looking south, the entire city of Chang'an unfolded before you, the Danfeng Gate, Vermilion Bird Street, and Mingde Gate aligned in sequence. You can imagine the Zhenguan court in session: Qin Qiong, Yuchi Gong, Cheng Yaojin, and other generals of Wagang origin standing in the Hanyuan Hall in court robes, holding ivory tablets — once wild rustic heroes who devoured meat and drank wine in great gulps at Wagang Stockade, now founding fathers of the Great Tang. Li Shimin's line — "The strong wind reveals the tough grass; a turbulent age shows the truly loyal" — was spoken of them. The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda was built under Xuanzang's direction in the third year of Yonghui (652 AD) to house the sutras and Buddhist images he brought back from India. Originally five stories, it was raised to ten by Empress Wu, then after war damage it was rebuilt as the present seven stories, standing 64.5 meters tall. The pagoda is a square brick pyramid, each side of every story having a brick arch doorway, with a spiral staircase ascending through the interior. Standing at the top of the pagoda and looking north, the outline of the Daming Palace is faintly visible — two buildings separated by the streets of Chang'an, one the pinnacle of worldly power, the other the high ground of spiritual faith. And the story of Qin Qiong and Yuchi Gong was also elevated between these two buildings: from bearing arms at Xuanwu Gate of the Daming Palace to becoming the door-god images pasted on the front doors of countless ordinary homes — heroes need not dwell in history books; it is enough that they live on the door panels of the people. Chang'an may have become Xi'an, the Daming Palace may have become ruins, the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda may have become a tourist attraction, but Qin Qiong and Yuchi Gong will forever stand at the first glance when you open your door — what they guard is every Chinese person's simplest wish for peace and safety.

stops.title: Stop Three: Luoyang · Empress Wu's Dragon Gate in a Former Life
stops.content: In the Sui and Tang periods, Luoyang and Chang'an were the two capitals. Emperor Yang of Sui excavated the Grand Canal, and Luoyang, situated at the center of the realm, saw a steady stream of boats from north and south. After Empress Wu Zetian ascended the throne, she made Luoyang the capital and changed the dynasty's name to Zhou, becoming China's only female emperor. South of Luoyang, the Longmen Grottoes represent the pinnacle of Sui-Tang stone carving art. On the cliffs along both banks of the Yi River, over two thousand niches and more than one hundred thousand Buddha statues create a magnificent spectacle. The Vairocana Buddha in the Fengxian Temple stands seventeen meters tall, said to have been modeled on Empress Wu herself — a face of compassion and authority, looking down on the rise and fall of the world, and on the joys and sorrows of the Sui-Tang heroes. Below the grottoes, the Yi River flows quietly, washing away a thousand years of flashing blades, leaving only the Buddha's compassion. The Longmen Grottoes were first carved in the Northern Wei Xiaowen Emperor's reign (493 AD) and continued through the Eastern Wei, Western Wei, Northern Qi, Sui, and Tang dynasties — a span of over four hundred years of continuous carving. The most awe-inspiring site is the Fengxian Temple, carved into the mountain itself — about thirty-six meters wide from east to west and forty meters deep from north to south. The main figure, Vairocana, stands 17.14 meters tall, with ears alone 1.9 meters long. The Buddha's face is full and rounded, the eyebrows curved like crescent moons, the eyes slightly downcast, the lips bearing a faint hint of a smile — simultaneously majestic and compassionate, distant and approachable. Legend has it that Empress Wu donated twenty thousand strings of cash from her cosmetic allowance to fund the construction, and the artisans used her face as the model for Vairocana — if true, the only female emperor in history achieved a form of "immortality" through this means. Flanking Vairocana on either side stand his disciples Kasyapa and Ananda, the bodhisattvas Manjushri and Samantabhadra, and heavenly kings and vajra warriors — each over ten meters tall. The vajra warriors glare with wide eyes, their muscles bulging, the demons beneath their feet crushed and grimacing in agony — this kind of intense emotional tension was unprecedented before the Tang dynasty. Standing on the platform before Fengxian Temple and looking up, with the sun slanting from the southeast, Vairocana's face is half in light, half in shadow, the expression sometimes compassionate, sometimes profound — just like Empress Wu herself, half a devout Buddhist, half a cold-hearted politician. If the heroes of the Romance of the Sui and Tang stood here, they would understand: no matter how sharp the sword, it cannot cut through a Buddha's smile. The Yi River has flowed quietly beneath the cliffs for thousands of years, washing away so much hero's blood, but unable to wash away the Buddha's compassion. And the White Horse Temple has stood silent watch east of Luoyang for two thousand years — this first ancient temple of China witnessed the entire journey of Buddhism from the Western Regions into the central plains, and witnessed the four hundred years from the first chisel stroke at Longmen to the last brushstroke of color. From the morning bells of White Horse Temple to the evening drums of Longmen Grottoes, Luoyang blended the Buddha's compassion with the hero's blood and spirit.

stops.title: Stop Four: Yangzhou · Sui Dike Willows in the Moonlight
stops.content: Emperor Yang of Sui expended the full strength of the empire to excavate the Grand Canal and traveled to Yangzhou three times to see the qionghua blossoms. His dragon boat stretched for a thousand li, and the misty willows planted along both banks stretched on without end — "Ten thousand dragon boats amidst green silk, carrying him to Yangzhou, never to return." The canal brought three centuries of prosperity to Yangzhou and drew countless heroes to leave their footprints here. The Garden of Individuality in Yangzhou was a Qing-dynasty salt merchant's private garden, named for its bamboos and defined by its rocks, with four-season rockeries each possessing its own charm. And the Lotus Bridge and White Pagoda on Slender West Lake were built in the Qianlong reign to welcome the emperor on his southern tour — the Five-Pavilion Bridge lies gracefully across the blue waves, the White Pagoda stands tall and elegant. The sound of the canal's waters, the bamboo shadows of the gardens, the gentle breeze on Slender West Lake — all weave together into Yangzhou's unique poetic atmosphere. Emperor Yang's dragon boat has long sunk into the depths of time, but the prosperity along both banks of the canal has continued unbroken for a thousand years. Emperor Yang of Sui, Yang Guang, is one of the most complex figures in the Romance of the Sui and Tang. His grand vision completed the Grand Canal, a wonder of world engineering history, yet his boundless debauchery ultimately lost the Sui dynasty its throne. In the first year of Daye (605 AD), he ordered the excavation of the Tongji Canal, connecting the Yellow River and the Huai River, and in the same year excavated the Hangou to connect the Huai and the Yangtze — a total length of over two thousand li. After the canal was completed, he sailed the dragon boat south to Yangzhou — the boat stood forty-five feet high and two hundred feet long, with four decks, accompanied by thousands of vessels and over eighty thousand trackers. Li Shangyin wrote a poem in lament: "He went south on a whim, no one dared remonstrate; across the land, imperial brocade was cut — half for saddle cloths, half for sails." The empire's entire resources were devoted to making brocade — half for under-saddle padding, half for the sails. Yet the irony is that Emperor Yang never lived to see the qionghua blossoms of Yangzhou he so desired. The canal he excavated with the full force of the realm instead became the lifeblood of the Tang dynasty's three centuries of glory. Standing on Five-Pavilion Bridge, the ripples of Slender West Lake reflect not the dragon boat's image, but the unending stream of pleasure boats — the canal still flows, Yangzhou's prosperity continues. The contrast between Emperor Yang of Sui and Li Shimin is like an eternal fable: both mobilized the full strength of the nation — one used it for personal pleasure, the other for governance. The Romance of the Sui and Tang fully captures this cycle of becoming, dwelling, decaying, and vanishing — the fall of Sui was the beginning of emptiness, the rise of Tang was the continuation of fulfillment. And Yangzhou, at the crossroads of the canal and the Yangtze, became the best seat in the house for this grand historical drama.

stops.title: Stop Five: Wagang Stockade · True Worth Knows No Rank
stops.content: Cheng Yaojin fixed Wagang with three axe-strokes; the Rogue Emperor sat on the golden throne. Wagang Stockade is the most thrilling stage in the Romance of the Sui and Tang. Qin Qiong sells his horse, Luo Cheng wins the championship, Shan Xiongxin gathers the brotherhood — the rustic heroes of the wilds relied on their skills and acted on their principles in a chaotic age. Though the Wagang army ultimately disbanded, those vivid faces — Cheng Yaojin's simple honesty, Qin Qiong's loyalty, Xu Maogong's cunning — have long since transcended the dust of history to become the template for "true men" in the Chinese imagination. The exact location of Wagang Stockade is in present-day Hua County, Henan. Though it has no dedicated national heritage site, the Yinxu Ruins in Anyang lie within the Wagang army's sphere of activity — this ancient Shang capital witnessed, in the Sui-Tang period, a new cycle of heroic emergence. From Shang-Zhou to Sui-Tang, the rise and fall of dynasties played out repeatedly on this land. Though the Wagang heroes chose different fates — some became founding fathers of the state, others met noble deaths — the strain of heroic spirit that "cries out against injustice when the road is rough" remained the most stirring keynote of the Romance of the Sui and Tang. The core stories of the Wagang army cluster in the middle section of the Romance — the most blood-stirring chapters of the entire book. Zhai Rang founded the Wagang army, Li Mi joined and usurped power, Qin Qiong and Cheng Yaojin drifted into Tang allegiance. Wagang was not merely a military stronghold; it was a great crucible of character. Here, the rustic met strategy (Xu Maogong), recklessness met restraint (Qin Qiong), personal grievances met the greater cause of the realm (Cheng Yaojin). Chu Renhuo gave Cheng Yaojin the most amusing segment in the novel — this "Rogue Emperor" who could barely read a word somehow ended up on the Wagang chieftain's throne, and his only policy achievement during his tenure was: "Brothers, where do we hit today?" Though the historical Wagang army disintegrated under Li Mi, the talent it nurtured became the core founding team of the Tang dynasty. Xu Shiji (the novel's Xu Maogong) was later granted the imperial surname Li and renamed Li Ji, becoming one of the twenty-four meritorious officials of Lingyan Pavilion; Qin Qiong rose to General of the Left Guard; Cheng Yaojin (original name Cheng Zhijie) lived to the age of ninety. Wagang dissolved, but Wagang's men scattered into every strategic pass of the Tang. Standing on the earthen platform of the Yinxu Ruins and looking east — this is the very land where the Wagang army once thundered past. The Shang-dynasty chariot pits lie silent beneath your feet; the hoofbeats of Sui-Tang surge in the wind. Three thousand years ago, Fu Hao led armies into battle; fourteen hundred years ago, Cheng Yaojin cleared the road with his axe — the heroic spirit of the Central Plains has never been broken.

stops.title: Stop Six: Zhaoling and Qianling · The Achievements and Faults of a Thousand Ages
stops.content: In the twenty-third year of Zhenguan (649 AD), Emperor Taizong of Tang, Li Shimin, died and was buried at the Zhaoling Mausoleum on Mount Jiuzong. He initiated the Tang practice of tunneling into a natural mountain for the burial chamber — the mausoleum grounds stretched sixty kilometers in circumference, with over one hundred and eighty satellite tombs. The Zhaoling Six Steeds reliefs are an unparalleled treasure of stone carving: six warhorses that had accompanied Li Shimin on his campaigns were forever frozen in stone — Saluzi, Quanmaogua, Baitiwu — each one corresponding to a chapter of martial adventure. And the Qianling Mausoleum on Mount Liang is even more legendary — the joint burial of Tang Gaozong, Li Zhi, and Empress Wu Zetian, the only imperial mausoleum in Chinese history interring two emperors. The blank stele stands beside the spirit-way, its surface bare, left for every generation to judge. Zhaoling and Qianling gaze at each other from afar — two emperors, the achievements and faults of a thousand ages, left for posterity to discuss. The stories of the Sui-Tang heroes all ultimately turned into the silent earth at the foot of the Qinling Mountains. The Zhaoling Mausoleum pioneered the Chinese imperial practice of using a natural mountain as the tomb. The main peak of Mount Jiuzong was tunneled to create the burial chamber, at an altitude of 1,188 meters, requiring one to look up to see the summit. The mausoleum grounds stretched 12.5 kilometers from north to south and 10 kilometers from east to west, studded with satellite tombs — including those of Wei Zheng, Fang Xuanling, Qin Qiong, Yuchi Gong, Cheng Yaojin, Li Jing, and other founding officials. The tombs of military officers were in the northwest of the grounds, those of civil officials in the southeast — even after death, Li Shimin was still governing the realm. The most breathtaking are the Zhaoling Six Steeds — six stone panels, each about 1.7 meters high and 2 meters wide, carved with the six warhorses Li Shimin rode on his campaigns. On the Saluzi relief, the general Qiu Xinggong bends down to pull an arrow from the horse's chest. The horse lowered its head in agony, but its eyes showed no fear — the life-and-death trust between a warhorse and its general was carved into stone by Tang artisans with a single chisel. Sadly, two of the six (Saluzi and Quanmaogua) were stolen in 1914 and sold to the University of Pennsylvania Museum in the United States. Standing in the Zhaoling Museum and looking at the remaining four steeds, the sense of incompleteness is more piercing than wholeness. Drive northwest from Zhaoling for less than a hundred li and you reach the Qianling Mausoleum — Empress Wu's Qianling. The spirit-way rises gently from south to north following the mountain's contours, flanked by over one hundred stone statues: ornamental pillars, winged horses, ostriches, stone horses, stone men... The most striking are the sixty-one stone statues of foreign officials — they represent envoys from Western Regions states who came to attend Gaozong's funeral, but all their heads have been destroyed, for reasons unknown. Standing before the blank stele and looking up at this enormous monument — 7.53 meters high, weighing about one hundred tons — the surface is indeed blank, but the top is carved with eight coiling hornless dragons, the sides with cloud-dragon patterns. The blankness was not due to Wu Zetian's modesty, but to her confidence — merit and fault need no written proof; history will give its own judgment. Zhaoling and Qianling are only a few dozen li apart. From Li Shimin to Wu Zetian, from the Zhenguan Golden Age to the High Tang Prime — two mountains, two mausoleums, two restless souls, together holding up the Tang dynasty, the most splendid dream in the Chinese heart. The gold and iron of the Sui-Tang heroes have all returned to the earth of the Qinling Mountains. But when the wind blows past the mausoleums, you can distinctly hear the sound of hoofbeats, the clash of swords, and the great laugh of Cheng Yaojin.
